title: Helvetica
hook: A Swiss typeface from 1957 that quietly ended up on signs all over the world.
peek: Helvetica began in 1957 at a small Swiss type foundry under another name. Renamed after the Latin word for Switzerland, it spread to subway signs, airline logos and computer screens, and became so common people stopped seeing it.
lede: In 1957, Max Miedinger and Eduard Hoffmann of the Haas Type Foundry near Basel released a plain, even sans-serif called Neue Haas Grotesk. A few years later it was renamed Helvetica, from Helvetia, the Latin name for Switzerland, to sell abroad. It went on to become one of the most widely used typefaces ever made.

bullets.text: The original name sounded too local for export. The German foundry Stempel, working with Linotype, chose Helvetica in 1960, and the international name helped the design travel.
The New York City subway's signs have long been tied to Helvetica. Early signs mixed it with similar typefaces, and the transit authority later made Helvetica its standard.

Arial, released in 1982, was drawn with the same letter widths as Helvetica, so a document could swap one for the other without reflowing. Designers still argue about the small differences in letters like R and t.
In 2007 Helvetica got its own feature-length documentary, made by Gary Hustwit to mark the typeface's 50th anniversary. It is rare for a font to be the star of a film.
Helvetica belongs to the Swiss or International Style of design, with clean grids and lots of white space. It shares its love of order with modernist painters like Piet Mondrian.
Type shapes language. When early English printers used type sets from the Continent, they lacked a letter for thorn, which helped give us the mistaken Ye of Ye Olde.
